definition: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: a pattern in which relevant external knowledge is retrieved and supplied to an LLM so that its response can be grounded in that knowledge.
RAG in which an agent or agent workflow can plan retrieval, choose retrieval tools or sources, reformulate queries, and synthesize evidence.
The process of finding potentially relevant information from a corpus in response to a query.
Retrieval based on semantic similarity between a query and stored representations, rather than relying only on exact keyword matches.
Search over vector representations to find items that are mathematically close to a query vector.
A numerical vector representation of text or another object that captures useful semantic characteristics for similarity-based search.
A model that converts text or other inputs into vector representations.
A database or index designed to store and search vector representations, usually together with the associated content and metadata.
A vector database commonly used for storing embeddings and supporting vector similarity search.
A semantically meaningful portion of a source document used as a unit for retrieval and downstream processing.
The process of dividing a document into retrieval-sized pieces while trying to preserve useful semantic boundaries.
Chunking that uses meaning, topic or document structure as the primary boundary rather than cutting purely by character or token count.
A unit of text processed by an LLM; token counts are used to reason about context limits and processing cost.
The amount of tokenized input and output context an LLM can handle within a request or processing context.
A second-stage retrieval step that reorders an initial set of retrieved candidates using a more precise relevance model or scoring method.
Retrieval that combines multiple retrieval mechanisms, commonly semantic/vector search with lexical or metadata-based search.
Restricting retrieval candidates using structured metadata such as source, topic, document type, date or authority.
Transforming an original user query into one or more retrieval-oriented queries to improve recall or relevance.
An architecture that retrieves from multiple corpora or knowledge sources, potentially using routing to decide which sources to query.
Constraining an LLM response using retrieved evidence or other authoritative context rather than relying only on model-internal knowledge.
An LLM-generated statement that is unsupported, fabricated, or inconsistent with the available evidence.
A change in the underlying knowledge over time that can make previously indexed or retrieved information stale.
How current the information available to a retrieval system is relative to the source of truth or the intended use.
A retriever designed for a particular source, content type, query class or retrieval strategy.
The collection of source material made available to the RAG system for retrieval.
A corpus containing multiple source formats or types, such as transcripts, PDFs, webpages, notes and slides.
The deterministic or source-specific process of extracting content and structure from an original source.
Extraction of headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, timestamps, speakers and other structural elements before semantic enrichment.
LLM-assisted transformation that adds topics, concepts, entities, classifications and other controlled metadata while preserving source evidence.
A consistent Markdown representation used as the common intermediate format for heterogeneous source documents.
A YAML metadata block placed at the beginning of a Markdown document to store document-level metadata.
Removing transcription noise and improving readability while preserving the substantive meaning and provenance of the original conversation.
A meeting transcript containing conversational content, often with speaker and timestamp information, used as a source for the RAG corpus.
Information identifying which speaker contributed a piece of transcript content.
The timestamp associated with transcript content, allowing retrieved information to be traced back to the original point in the recording or transcript.
A predefined set of permitted terms used to make classification and metadata values consistent.
A managed collection of terms and definitions used as a shared vocabulary for the corpus and its semantic enrichment.
Assigning topic or subject labels to content to support organization, filtering and retrieval.
Identifying named or meaningful entities in source content, such as technologies, organizations, people or concepts.
A stable identifier for a source document that allows the document and its derived chunks or records to be linked.
A stable identifier for an individual chunk derived from a source document.
Structured information describing a document, chunk, entity or other data object, such as source, topic, owner, timestamp or document type.
Information describing where a piece of information came from and how it relates to its source.
Metadata describing the evidentiary basis and characteristics of knowledge, such as source authority, trust, freshness and supporting evidence.
A record of relationships showing where data or derived content came from and how it moved or was transformed.
A score or classification intended to represent the perceived reliability or authority of a source or derived knowledge item.
A quantitative or categorical assessment of the quality of a data object or corpus item according to defined quality criteria.
An indication of how authoritative a source is for a particular subject or claim.
The designated authoritative source for a particular fact, data element or business concept.
An open-source metadata platform considered as a catalog and governance layer for the RAG corpus and related AI assets.
A system that stores and exposes metadata about data assets, documents, ownership, relationships and other governed objects.
A governed collection of business terms and their meanings, often linked to data assets and physical representations.
Critical Data Element: a data element identified as especially important to a business process, reporting, risk, compliance or other organizational objective.
The discipline and set of measures used to assess whether data is fit for its intended purpose.
The degree to which retrieved or enriched content preserves the intended meaning and relationships of the source.
The managed stages through which a document, chunk, metadata record or AI asset progresses, such as creation, enrichment, use, review and retirement.
A database optimized for representing entities and relationships and traversing those relationships.
A graph-based representation of entities, concepts and relationships that makes explicit how pieces of knowledge are connected.
A RAG approach that uses graph-structured knowledge or relationships alongside retrieval to answer questions requiring connected concepts or multi-hop relationships.
A typed connection between two entities or concepts in a graph.
A graph representing relationships among concepts extracted from or associated with source material.
Retrieval that follows multiple relationships or steps to assemble evidence needed for a query.
A governed layer containing searchable content, metadata, relationships and other structured knowledge that agents can access.
A memory approach in which information is stored and retrieved according to explicit structures and rules rather than being reconstructed solely by an LLM.
Large Language Model: a model trained on large text corpora to perform language understanding and generation tasks.
A relatively small Qwen language model used in the capstone as a local model for bounded semantic enrichment and classification tasks.
A language model executed locally rather than through a remote hosted inference service.
A constrained LLM task with a defined output purpose and scope, such as classification, tagging or entity extraction.
Non-real-time LLM enrichment performed independently of an interactive user request, allowing processing to be batched and monitored.
A predefined confidence level used to decide whether an automated model output can be accepted or should be reviewed or escalated.
A workflow that routes uncertain, failed or high-risk cases from a smaller or automated model to human review or a stronger model.
Checking model or program output against a predefined structure and allowed fields or values.
Model output constrained to a predefined structure, often JSON or a typed schema, so downstream software can process it reliably.
The instructions and contextual input supplied to an LLM for a task.
Breaking a larger task into multiple model calls whose outputs are passed between steps.
Providing examples in a prompt to demonstrate the expected behavior or output format.
A workflow in which one model step generates an output and another step critiques or evaluates it before refinement.
An iterative pattern where a model evaluates and improves its own generated output using explicit feedback or criteria.
A rule, validator or control designed to constrain model behavior or prevent unsafe, invalid or unwanted outputs.
A software system that uses an LLM or other reasoning component to decide actions, use tools, manage state and pursue a defined objective.
AI systems designed to perform multi-step tasks with some degree of planning, reasoning, tool use and autonomous execution.
The sequence of reasoning, retrieval, tool use, state changes and other steps through which an agent performs a task.
A component that coordinates multiple steps, tools or agents and controls how work moves through a workflow.
An architecture in which an orchestrator delegates tasks to specialized worker components and aggregates their results.
A component that classifies an input and selects an appropriate downstream path, tool, retriever or agent.
An agent pattern in which planning and execution are separated so a plan can be generated and then carried out through tools or workers.
A workflow in which an evaluator scores an output and an optimizer uses the evaluation to improve it.
An agent that coordinates other agents, assigns work and handles escalation or synthesis.
A system in which multiple specialized agents cooperate or coordinate to solve a larger task.
A design pattern in which a human reviews, approves, corrects or takes over specific automated decisions or actions.
An agent capability in which the model selects and invokes external functions, APIs, databases or services.
A mechanism through which an LLM produces structured arguments for a predefined function or tool invocation.
Model Context Protocol: a protocol pattern for exposing tools and contextual resources to AI models and agents through standardized interfaces.
An architecture in which agents can access a network of shared tools or services through standardized interfaces.
Information maintained across workflow steps so an agent or orchestrator can track task progress and context.
Persisted or temporary information used by an agent beyond the immediate prompt context.
Memory representing general knowledge, concepts or facts that can be reused across sessions or tasks.
Memory representing experiences or events associated with particular interactions or episodes.
Memory representing how to perform tasks, procedures or workflows.
Connecting information across multiple interactions or sessions so context can persist over time.
The programming language used for the capstone implementation, AI workflows, data processing and supporting services.
A programming model that allows a program to initiate work that may wait for I/O without blocking other eligible work from progressing.
Python's standard library framework for writing asynchronous, concurrent I/O-oriented code using async/await.
A Python keyword used to define an asynchronous function or coroutine.
A Python keyword used inside asynchronous code to suspend execution until an awaitable operation completes.
An asynchronous computation represented by a Python function defined with async def that can suspend at await points.
A Python web framework used to build APIs, including lightweight services around AI or agent workflows.
An ASGI server commonly used to run Python web applications such as FastAPI services.
Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface: a Python interface for asynchronous web servers and applications.
A Python library for defining typed data models and validating structured data.
A typed schema defined with Pydantic that validates and structures input or output data.
A Python testing framework used to write and run automated unit and integration tests.
Application Programming Interface: a defined interface through which software components communicate or request capabilities or data.
An architectural style commonly used for web APIs using resources, HTTP methods and stateless requests.
An API query language and runtime that allows clients to request structured data through a typed schema.
Create, Read, Update and Delete: the basic operations commonly supported by data-oriented applications and APIs.
Structured Query Language used to query and manipulate relational data.
A pattern in which natural-language requests are translated into SQL queries for structured data retrieval.
Techniques for detecting, catching and managing runtime errors so applications can fail safely or recover.
Repeating a failed operation according to defined rules, often with limits or delays.
A maximum permitted duration for an operation before it is treated as failed or abandoned.
A restriction on how frequently an API, model or service can be called within a period.
A property whereby repeating the same operation produces the same intended end state as performing it once.
Systematic measurement of retrieval and generation quality against defined evaluation criteria and datasets.
A framework used to evaluate RAG systems using metrics for aspects such as retrieval and answer quality.
A curated reference dataset containing expected or trusted examples used to evaluate system behavior.
Evaluation examples generated programmatically or with models rather than collected solely from real user interactions.
Evaluation of individual stages of an AI workflow, such as retrieval, tool selection or synthesis, rather than only the final answer.
Evaluation focused on whether the final system output achieves the desired result.
The relationship between system quality and the computational, model, latency or operational cost required to achieve it.
The ability to understand system behavior through traces, logs, metrics and other operational signals.
Recording the sequence and timing of operations through a workflow so execution can be inspected and diagnosed.
Recording structured or textual events produced by an application for debugging, auditing and operational analysis.
Quantitative measurements of system behavior such as latency, errors, token usage or retrieval performance.
Tracking input and output token consumption to understand cost, capacity and model behavior.
An attack or failure mode in which untrusted input attempts to manipulate an LLM into ignoring intended instructions or performing unintended actions.
Personally Identifiable Information: information that can identify or reasonably be linked to an individual.
Adversarial testing intended to discover weaknesses, unsafe behavior or failure modes in an AI system.
Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery/Deployment: automated practices for building, testing and releasing software.
A deployment strategy that maintains two environments so traffic can be shifted between an existing version and a new version with controlled rollback.
Returning a deployed system to a previous known version after a problematic release.
Packaging an application and its dependencies into a portable container image for consistent deployment.
A platform and tooling ecosystem for building and running containerized applications.
A framework used to build LLM applications and workflows, including chains, tools and retrieval components.
A framework focused on connecting LLM applications with external data, indexing and retrieval workflows.
A framework for building stateful, graph-based agent workflows and multi-step orchestration.
A framework for orchestrating multiple specialized AI agents working together on tasks.
A document-processing tool discussed for extracting PDF structure into Markdown or other structured representations.
